question: Does feature-learning training prioritize easy examples more strongly than an initialization-linearized neural network, and can a solvable quadratic parameterization explain the resulting order of clean, noisy, and spuriously correlated examples?

key_findings.claim: Across several operational definitions, feature-learning runs spread the learning times of easy and difficult groups more than near-linearized runs.
key_findings.evidence: A yin-yang toy task, CIFAR-10 C-score deciles, and CIFAR-10 with 15% random label flips are compared at matched aggregate or clean-example loss. Standard alpha=1 networks reduce losses on large/simple regions, high-C-score examples, and clean labels earlier relative to alpha=100 copies. VGG11, changed initialization/minibatch seeds, accuracy plots, and learning-rate sweeps show the same qualitative ordering.

anchors.section: E Interplay between learning rate and alpha scaling

key_findings.claim: The claimed feature-learning contrast is better supported than a simple learning-rate explanation, but alpha is not a pure intervention on one causal mechanism.
key_findings.evidence: The rescaled predictor f_alpha=f_0+alpha(f-f_0) and learning rate eta/alpha^2 keep first-order function updates comparable. At alpha=100, activation signs, empirical NTK alignment, and representation alignment remain near initialization, whereas alpha=1 changes all three. A four-order learning-rate sweep at alpha=1 does not reproduce the alpha-dependent group trajectories. Nevertheless alpha also changes parameter displacement, higher-order terms, effective noise/regularization, numerical conditioning, and the realized finite-width function class during optimization, so 'feature learning caused the ordering' is an interpretation rather than an isolated causal fact.

anchors.section: E Interplay between learning rate and alpha scaling

key_findings.claim: Feature learning's early-example bias can help with label noise yet hurt worst-group robustness when the easiest pattern is spurious.
key_findings.evidence: On random-label CIFAR-10, alpha=1 delays fitting flipped labels and attains a better early-stopped test-loss sweet spot. On CelebA blond-hair/gender and Waterbirds bird/background correlations, alpha=1 and alpha=0.5 learn majority/spurious groups sooner, while alpha=100 initially has higher balanced-test and non-spurious-group accuracy. This is an important qualification: faster 'easy' learning is not synonymous with better generalization.

key_findings.claim: A diagonally factorized quadratic linear predictor gives an exact mode-wise mechanism for nonlinear sequentialization.
key_findings.evidence: Writing theta as one-half the sum of squared mode parameters makes gradient flow logistic in each input singular direction. Its effective kernel eigenvalue grows with the squared parameter, so the nonlinear convergence exponent is proportional to the input-label correlation component sqrt(mu_lambda)y_lambda; the linearized exponent instead freezes at mu_lambda theta_0lambda. In the vanishing-initialization limit, stronger nonlinear modes finish before weaker ones depart initialization.

anchors.section: A Details on the theoretical analysis

key_findings.claim: The closed-form theory proves a property of a specially aligned quadratic parameterization, not of generic deep ReLU feature learning.
key_findings.evidence: The parameterization squares one independent scalar per right singular vector of the complete training matrix and therefore builds the data SVD into the model coordinates. It uses least-squares gradient flow, nonnegative target-mode coordinates, small balanced initialization, and decoupled modes. The empirical networks use cross-entropy, convolution, SGD, finite steps, and learned representations. Figure 14 gives qualitative support from a dense two-layer MLP, but no approximation theorem connects it to ResNet18/CIFAR dynamics.

key_findings.claim: The convergence-time ratio printed in the discussion is inverted.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 14 gives t_lambda approximately proportional to 1/tilde-y_lambda, up to mode-dependent logarithms. It follows that t_lambda/t_lambda-prime is approximately tilde-y_lambda-prime/tilde-y_lambda, not tilde-y_lambda/tilde-y_lambda-prime as the next paragraph states. The surrounding qualitative claim that larger tilde-y modes are faster and Equation 15's ordering agree with the reciprocal, so this appears to be a local algebraic typo rather than a failure of Proposition 1.

key_findings.claim: Matching runs by an endogenous loss coordinate is useful for ordering analysis but cannot answer efficiency or endpoint-performance questions by itself.
key_findings.evidence: The alpha=1 CIFAR C-score run trains 200 epochs while alpha=100 trains 1,000, then curves are reparameterized by mean training loss; noisy-label curves are matched by clean-example loss and spurious-group plots condition on with-spurious accuracy. These comparisons ask which groups are learned at equal selected progress. They discard wall-clock/step efficiency, can condition on a mediator affected by the regime, and do not compare models at matched compute, matched validation rule, or identical stopping information.

key_findings.claim: The empirical breadth is meaningful but statistical reporting remains mostly visual.
key_findings.evidence: The appendix changes architecture, initialization, minibatch order, and learning rate, and the toy experiment averages 100 initializations. For the real-data results, however, plots provide individual trajectories without a prespecified scalar schedule-separation statistic, confidence interval, seed aggregate, hypothesis test, effect size, or sensitivity to difficulty-score uncertainty. CelebA uses only 20,000 training examples and balanced subsets of 180 per group; Waterbirds likewise uses small minority groups.

method.core_idea: Interpolate a fixed finite network between standard and lazy training with output scaling, compare group learning trajectories at matched progress, and explain differences through exact gradient flow in a mode-factorized quadratic model.
method.mechanism: Clone an initialized network; replace its output displacement by alpha times that displacement and scale learning rate by alpha squared; diagnose laziness through ReLU-sign, NTK, and representation Gram alignment; track losses/accuracies for difficulty groups; then diagonalize a least-squares problem and compare logistic nonlinear mode dynamics with the frozen-kernel exponential dynamics.
assumptions: Large alpha plus near-unit linearity metrics is a faithful finite-width proxy for training the exact initialization linearization.
Output and learning-rate rescaling makes the regimes comparable in function-space progress.
Aggregate-loss or selected-group-loss matching is the relevant definition of equal training progress.
C-score deciles, corrupted labels, and majority/spurious groups are valid operational notions of example difficulty.
Group loss trajectories reflect resource prioritization rather than only calibration or margin scaling.
The simple quadratic mode dynamics preserve the mechanism that matters in deep convolutional networks.
Seed and architecture checks shown visually cover the main sources of empirical variation.
Early stopping is available when schedule differences are translated into generalization benefits.

techniques.role: Continuously reduces parameter motion while keeping first-order function updates comparable.
Checks whether the tangent kernel remains close to initialization.
Tracks adaptation of the penultimate feature geometry.
Separates losses and accuracies by C-score, label corruption, or spurious-group status.
Compares regimes at equal aggregate or reference-group learning progress.
Produces exact nonlinear and frozen-linear gradient-flow solutions per input singular mode.

evaluations.setting: Four-layer ReLU MLP on a 2D yin-yang dataset over 100 initializations
evaluations.metric: test-point loss difference at matched training-loss thresholds
evaluations.result: feature learning favors large simple regions while linearization favors intricate boundary/island regions
evaluations.baseline: alpha=100 copy from the same initialization

evaluations.setting: ResNet18 and VGG11 on CIFAR-10 grouped by C-score
evaluations.metric: per-decile training/test loss and accuracy versus mean training loss
evaluations.result: feature-learning trajectories show greater separation between high- and low-C-score groups

evaluations.metric: noisy-label loss/accuracy and clean test performance at matched clean loss
evaluations.result: feature learning delays corrupted-label memorization and reaches a better early-stopped test sweet spot

evaluations.setting: CelebA blond/gender and Waterbirds class/background correlations
evaluations.metric: with- versus without-spurious group accuracy during training
evaluations.result: feature-learning runs fit majority/spurious groups earlier and initially underperform the linearized run on balanced/minority evaluation

evaluations.setting: Constructed quadratic regression and label-noise/spurious-feature examples
evaluations.result: nonlinear rates depend on input-label correlation and sequentialize under small initialization; frozen-linear rates depend on initial kernel eigenvalues

limitations: Alpha scaling changes more than feature adaptation and is not a perfectly isolated causal intervention.
The main real-data comparisons use a near-linearized finite network rather than explicitly training the exact linear model in Equation 3.
Progress normalization answers a conditional ordering question, not matched-compute training efficiency.
Difficulty is definition-dependent; high C-score, clean label, and majority spurious correlation encode distinct concepts.
The phrase 'easy examples' can obscure that easy spurious groups are precisely the harmful ones for robust generalization.
Most empirical effects are assessed visually without aggregate effect sizes or uncertainty intervals.
Experiments center on older small vision benchmarks, ResNet18/VGG11, and no data augmentation/batch-normalization training.
CelebA and Waterbirds results use small balanced group subsets and do not report worst-group confidence intervals.
The theory hard-codes data singular vectors into a quadratic parameterization and does not cover ReLU/convnet feature learning.
The exact theory is least-squares gradient flow, whereas experiments use minibatch SGD and classification losses.
The printed nonlinear convergence-time ratio is reversed relative to Equation 14.
No intervention uses the discovered schedule to improve robustness, curriculum, reweighting, or stopping.
failure_modes: Equal-loss matching conditions on a regime-dependent mediator and creates a misleading apparent tradeoff between groups.
Alpha=100 optimization is so slow or ill-conditioned that incomplete convergence is mistaken for a different inductive bias.
Kernel/representation alignment near one hides small changes concentrated in a task-critical eigenspace.
C-score bins encode class, duplication, or acquisition artifacts rather than intrinsic example difficulty.
Feature learning prioritizes a shortcut and worsens minority accuracy even while aggregate loss improves faster.
Random-label memorization timing changes with augmentation, optimizer, normalization, width, or regularization and does not generalize.
Pretrained Waterbirds features already contain the relevant/spurious representations, blurring feature-learning versus head/kernel effects.
The quadratic model's aligned independent modes predict sequentialization that disappears with coupled nonlinear representations.
A single validation-based stopping rule cannot know which examples are corrupted or spuriously easy in deployment.
Group trajectories cross, so a conclusion based on one chosen loss threshold reverses later in training.
reusable_insights: Plot learning trajectories by example subgroup at matched progress as well as matched steps, compute, and wall time; the views answer different questions.
Treat feature adaptation as a schedule-shaping mechanism whose value depends on whether early-learned regularities are causal or spurious.
Use several laziness diagnostics because parameter distance, activation changes, kernel rotation, and representation change can disagree.
When deriving mode learning times, distinguish target alignment from input/kernel eigenvalues; nonlinear factorization can amplify the former.
Convert qualitative schedule claims into scalar preregistered measures such as group time-to-threshold gaps and integrate them over progress.
Audit coordinate/scaling interventions for optimizer-noise and regularization side effects before assigning causality to feature learning.
Use noisy-label delay only with a defensible early-stopping signal; otherwise both regimes can eventually memorize.
Pair any easy-first curriculum with shortcut/minority tests, since easy-first learning can be anti-robust.
open_questions: Does schedule separation persist in transformers, large pretrained models, and modern augmented/normed convnets at matched compute?
Can exact finite-width linearized baselines reproduce the alpha=100 results without its conditioning side effects?
Which measurable kernel or feature evolution predicts whether the early bias will favor robust versus spurious structure?
Can one derive generic coupled-mode theory beyond the data-aligned quadratic parameterization?
How do optimizer momentum, adaptive methods, batch noise, weight decay, normalization, and augmentation alter sequentialization?
Can schedule statistics detect label corruption or shortcut reliance without access to subgroup labels?
What stopping or reweighting policy uses the nonlinear-linear schedule gap to improve worst-group risk?
Are example-level difficulty rankings stable under representation learning, or must difficulty be modeled dynamically?

competitive_landscape.title: On Lazy Training in Differentiable Programming
competitive_landscape.difference: Chizat, Oyallon, and Bach establish how output scaling produces lazy optimization and bound closeness to linearized paths, while observing a vision performance gap. George et al. reuse that control to localize the gap in example-learning schedules rather than only final risk.

competitive_landscape.title: Limitations of Lazy Training of Two-layers Neural Network
competitive_landscape.relationship: Risk-gap theory between kernel and feature learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Ghorbani et al. prove sample/prediction-risk separations among random features, neural tangent, and fully trained two-layer networks on structured distributions. This paper gives a complementary temporal and example-group account, but with a much less general theorem.

competitive_landscape.title: Tensor Programs V: Tuning Large Neural Networks via Zero-Shot Hyperparameter Transfer
competitive_landscape.difference: Yang and Hu's maximal-update framework distinguishes parameterizations that retain feature learning at infinite width and supports hyperparameter transfer. It offers a scalable parameterization view beyond the finite alpha knob; the present paper instead focuses directly on which examples are learned first.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning sparse features can lead to overfitting in neural networks
competitive_landscape.relationship: Competing account of when feature learning hurts
competitive_landscape.difference: Paccolat et al. argue feature learning can overfit smooth image targets through sparse representations and compare mean-field with lazy predictors across sample sizes. George et al. identify an orthogonal early-training hazard: rapid uptake of easy spurious correlations and minority delay.

competitive_landscape.title: Mixed Dynamics In Linear Networks: Unifying the Lazy and Active Regimes
competitive_landscape.difference: Tu, Aranguri, and Jacot derive a mixed regime in which singular directions transition from lazy to active above a threshold, combining alignment and low-rank bias. This complicates a global lazy-versus-feature dichotomy and supplies a more general direction-wise theory than the paper's fixed two-regime quadratic example.

competitive_landscape.title: Distributionally Robust Neural Networks for Group Shifts: On the Importance of Regularization for Worst-Case Generalization
competitive_landscape.difference: Sagawa et al. benchmark Waterbirds/CelebA and optimize worst-group loss with regularization, directly targeting minority robustness. George et al. explain why ordinary feature-learning dynamics can initially worsen those groups, but do not turn the diagnosis into a robust training method.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: Nonlinear feature-learning dynamics impose a stronger easy-to-hard curriculum than lazy dynamics, explaining relative learning schedules across clean, noisy, and spuriously correlated examples.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The same qualitative schedule separation appears in a visual toy task, C-score bins, random labels, two spurious-correlation datasets, two architectures, several seeds, and an exactly solvable quadratic model.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The example-schedule lens is a genuinely useful and moderately novel complement to endpoint lazy-versus-feature comparisons. Its strongest result is descriptive: feature adaptation amplifies a hierarchy. The generic causal mechanism remains open because alpha is a composite intervention, comparisons condition on selected progress, and the theorem relies on a specially aligned quadratic model.

reviewer_notes: Read all 25 pages, including theoretical proofs, experimental details, every appendix figure, code description, and references. Re-derived Proposition 1's time scaling and found the reciprocal error in the prose immediately after Equation 14. Checked TMLR/OpenReview provenance and primary NeurIPS, ICML/PMLR, and arXiv competitors through 2026-08-23.
